thread.title: No. 1 Michigan hockey offense supported by faceoff improvements
thread.title_full: No. 1 Michigan hockey offense supported by faceoff improvements

author: Anna Liao
title: No. 1 Michigan hockey offense supported by faceoff improvements
text:
Six games into the season, it’s clear that the No. 1 Michigan hockey team still has one of the most explosive offenses in the nation. But it goes beyond flashy plays or sheer luck — the Wolverines’ scoring dominance starts with every faceoff.
“The offense is great,” Michigan coach Brandon Naurato said Oct. 17. “But everything away from the puck, (sophomore forward Cole McKinney and freshman forward Jack Nesbitt), the big faceoffs that they take every game. … It’s just such a luxury for a coach to have two guys like that.”
McKinney had the fifth-best faceoff win percentage in the Big Ten last year at 57.6%, and anchored the Wolverines’ third line and penalty kill with his consistency at the dot. It’s no surprise that he continues to bring the same success to Michigan this season — with 111 faceoffs under his belt already, McKinney has had plenty of chances to make his mark just as he did last season.
But after six games, it’s Nesbitt who claims the highest faceoff win percentage on the Wolverines’ roster with a 64.1% win rate after 103 draws. Nesbitt gives Michigan a solid chance to control the puck, regardless of the stakes.
In the Wolverines’ comeback win at Bowling Green State, Nesbitt logged a season-high 13 faceoff wins with just four losses. Nesbitt also helped Michigan break ground in its second game against then-No. 1 Denver. The Wolverines fired three back-to-back shots off a faceoff he won, scoring their first goal on one of those rebounds to tie the game.
In the same period as Nesbitt’s key faceoff, yet another forward followed suit when Michigan got its first powerplay opportunity of the night. From the Wolverines’ offensive faceoff circle, sophomore forward Adam Valentini drew the puck back, inching closer toward the net. It took just a few seconds and one well-placed shot for Valentini to score.
Nesbitt ranks fifth in the nation by faceoffs won — ahead of junior forward Michael Hage, who ranks eighth, and McKinney, who is tied for 10th.
“(Hage) has taken a huge step with his faceoffs this year,” Naurato said. “(McKinney and Nesbitt), that’s kind of what they do. It’s a specialty for them, but it’s still a five-man unit, so everyone just gets involved and helps those guys win it back.”
Michigan actually struggled to maintain its dominance in faceoffs against the Pioneers, requiring the rest of the five-man unit to keep up the pressure during play. Throughout both games in the series, Denver tallied more faceoff wins than the Wolverines, winning 52% and 55% of all faceoffs during the first and second games, respectively. To stay on top of the Pioneers without dominating possession from the get-go, Michigan instead took advantage of every rebound and played fast, aggressive defense.
The Wolverines’ all-around strength can nullify the issues that pop up when their opponent has more success on draws. Still, when Michigan struggles to win more faceoffs than its opponent, it shows. The Wolverines’ series victory against Denver went down to the wire. But Nesbitt and Valentini winning two crucial faceoffs in the first period certainly helped push Michigan over the Pioneers in the end.
For a star-studded roster with highly successful coaches to boot, anything less than sheer dominance would be disappointing. The Wolverines aren’t just outshooting their opponents or getting lucky at the net, though. Michigan aims to take control of the game from the moment the puck hits the ice. And with the help of its faceoffs, it’s well on its way there.
